questions.question: What does it mean that a Java String is immutable?
options: Its characters can never change after it is created
The variable holding it can never be reassigned
It can only store upper-case letters
It is always stored on the stack
questions.explanation: The String object itself never changes. The variable can still point to a different String later.

questions.question: What does this print? String a = "hub"; String b = "hub"; System.out.println(a == b);
questions.explanation: Both literals refer to the same object in the String pool, so the references are equal.

questions.question: What does this print? String a = "hub"; String c = new String("hub"); System.out.println(a == c);
questions.explanation: new String always creates a separate heap object, so the two references differ even though the text is the same.

questions.question: A user types "  yes ". Why does this check fail? String s = input; s.trim(); if (s.equals("yes")) { ... }
options: equals() ignores spaces only in Java 17
trim() removes only the first space
trim() returns a new String and the result was not stored
questions.explanation: Strings never change, so s.trim() alone is lost. Write s = s.trim(); before comparing.

questions.question: Where does Java keep string literals so that equal ones can be shared?
options: In the String pool inside the heap
In the class file only, never in memory
In a separate file on disk
questions.explanation: Literals are stored once in the String pool, which is part of the heap since Java 7.

questions.question: What does this print? String code = "parcel"; code.toUpperCase(); System.out.println(code);
questions.explanation: toUpperCase() returns a new String. The original variable still points to the lower-case text.

questions.question: Which class is the best choice for building a long text inside a loop in one thread?
questions.explanation: StringBuilder edits one buffer and has no locking cost, so it is the fastest option for a single thread.

questions.question: Why can this line crash? if (city.equals("Pune")) { ... } when city may be null.
options: equals() is not allowed on literals
Pune is not in the String pool
equals() must be written as equal()
Calling a method on null throws NullPointerException
questions.explanation: A null reference has no object to call equals() on. Writing "Pune".equals(city) avoids the crash.

questions.question: What does this print? System.out.println("TOLLGATE".substring(4, 8));
questions.explanation: substring(4, 8) takes indexes 4 to 7, the end index is excluded, which gives GATE.

questions.question: How does StringBuffer differ from StringBuilder?
options: StringBuffer methods are synchronized, so it is thread safe but slower
questions.explanation: Both are changeable, but StringBuffer locks on every call, which is safe for shared use and slower in one thread.
